text: This is the original pairing restricted to an additive subgroup H, with values still in ℚ/ℤ. An element of Lean’s subtype H is an element of A together with membership in H; the two projections merely forget those certificates. The restricted form can be degenerate even when A is nondegenerate, consistently with the finite-form convention in [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6). Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L453) passes, [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L591) passes.
The restricted pairing has exactly the original values on subgroup elements.
The restricted radical is H∩H⊥, so nondegeneracy is not silently inherited.

The equality says b_H(x,y)=b_A(x,y) for x,y∈H. The expressions x.1 and y.1 are the original group elements, not numerical coordinates. Thus restriction changes the allowed arguments and retains the ℚ/ℤ-valued pairing of [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6); no quotient or rescaling occurs. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L462) passes.
The inclusion sends each subgroup element to that same ambient element.

The group is unchanged and every pairing value is replaced by its additive inverse in ℚ/ℤ. This is the negative finite form of [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6). It does not negate both input vectors, which by bilinearity would leave the pairing unchanged; the evaluation and nondegeneracy controls distinguish the intended operation. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L472) passes, [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L475) passes.
The value is the negative of the original pairing.
Form negation preserves nondegeneracy in both directions.

This states b_{−A}(x,y)=−b_A(x,y) on the original group. The minus sign acts on the form value in ℚ/ℤ, not on x and y. That is the negative-form convention in [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6); the corresponding adjoint remains injective exactly when the original one is. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L475) passes.
The adjoint loses no information when its character values are negated.

The carrier is A×B and the pairing is b_A(x₁,y₁)+b_B(x₂,y₂), the orthogonal sum in [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6). For two factors the direct product and direct sum coincide. The displayed sum has no cross terms, so the two embedded factors are orthogonal; neither factor is assumed nondegenerate. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L499) passes, [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L542) passes.
The pairing is precisely the sum of the component pairings.
The radical is the product of the component radicals.

The coordinates x.1,x.2 and y.1,y.2 belong to the two factor groups. Their displayed pairing values add in ℚ/ℤ, giving the orthogonal-sum formula of [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6). Evaluating on (a,0) and (0,b) gives zero mixed pairing; this is not multiplication of the component values. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L542) passes.
Testing against each separate factor gives the product formula for radicals.

The kernel here is the kernel of x↦b(x,−): an element belongs precisely when it pairs to zero with every element of A. The zero character means zero modulo integers at every argument. This is the radical of a finite bilinear form in [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6), a subgroup rather than the set of vectors with only b(x,x)=0. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L527) passes.
Membership is exactly vanishing against every second argument.

Membership in the kernel of the pairing adjoint is unpacked as ∀y, b(x,y)=0 in ℚ/ℤ. Equality of characters means pointwise equality, so the quantifier checks every element, including x. This is precisely the radical condition for the finite forms of [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6), with no nondegeneracy assumption. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L538) passes.
The pointwise kernel condition gives the ordinary nondegeneracy criterion.

The symbol ⊥ denotes the subgroup {0}, not the empty set. A trivial adjoint kernel is equivalent to injectivity; the finite character group has the same order as A, making that equivalent to bijectivity. Thus Lean’s perfect-pairing definition agrees with radical-zero nondegeneracy for the forms of [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6), including the trivial group. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L148) passes.
Finite character duality identifies injectivity and bijectivity of this adjoint.

An element (x,y) is orthogonal to every pair exactly when x and y are orthogonal to their respective groups. Testing separately against (u,0) and (0,v) prevents cancellation from hiding a nonzero component. This gives rad(A⊥B)=rad(A)×rad(B) for the orthogonal-sum convention in [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6), including degenerate factors. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L499) passes.
The componentwise pairing gives both implications of the radical identity.

An orthogonal sum is nondegenerate exactly when both factors are: its radical is the product of their radicals, which is {0} exactly when each radical is {0}. This is the finite-form convention of [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6). No positivity or characteristic restriction appears, and a trivial factor is allowed. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L542) passes, [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L538) passes.
The radical product identity supplies the criterion.
Nondegeneracy is equivalent to trivial radical.

If x pairs to zero with every y, its adjoint character is the same as the character of zero. Injectivity supplied by nondegeneracy therefore gives x=0, exactly the radical-zero condition for [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6)’s finite forms. The hypothesis tests all y, not merely the self-pairing of x. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L570) passes.
The full subgroup of such elements is exactly {0}.

A perfect pairing has injective adjoint, so its kernel is {0}. Lean writes this subgroup as ⊥. This is the forward half of the ordinary radical criterion in [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6); it does not assert that a nonzero vector must have nonzero self-pairing. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L538) passes.
The equivalence records both directions of the exact radical criterion.

A zero radical makes x↦b(x,−) injective. Because A and its ℚ/ℤ-character group have equal finite cardinality, it is then bijective, which is Lean’s nondegeneracy condition. This recovers the finite perfect-pairing convention of [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6); the conclusion uses the full character group, not an arbitrarily chosen collection of characters. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L148) passes.
The finite-duality equivalence supplies surjectivity from injectivity.

H⊥ consists of the elements x of A for which b(x,h)=0 for every h∈H, in the finite-form convention of [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6). The conversion to an integer submodule only records repeated addition; it does not introduce a vector space or select representatives in ℚ. Symmetry reconciles the library’s argument order. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L582) passes, [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L612) passes.
The membership formula is exactly vanishing against every element of H.
For H=A this recovers the radical.

The formula says x∈H⊥ precisely when its pairing with every member of H vanishes in ℚ/ℤ. The two successive quantifiers mean “for every y belonging to H”, not “for every y in A”. Symmetry identifies this with the underlying integer-bilinear orthogonality definition, matching [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6). Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L606) passes, [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L612) passes.
The zero subgroup imposes no restriction, giving all of A.
Orthogonality to all of A is exactly its radical.

The radical of b restricted to S is S∩S⊥, considered as a subgroup of S. Lean’s addSubgroupOf expresses that intersection inside the smaller carrier; it does not assert that S⊥ is contained in S. This follows by testing the unchanged restricted pairing against every element of S, as in [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6)’s orthogonality convention. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L453) passes, [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L582) passes.
Restriction retains the original pairing on S.
Membership in S⊥ tests precisely the elements of S.

Every h∈H pairs to zero with each x∈H⊥ by symmetry, hence lies in H⊥⊥. The symbol ≤ is subgroup inclusion. Only inclusion is asserted: without nondegeneracy the reverse inclusion can fail, for example for a zero pairing. This matches orthogonality for the possibly degenerate forms of [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6). Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L582) passes.
The membership criterion and symmetry give the inclusion.

For a pairing-preserving group isomorphism f, the image f(H⊥) equals f(H)⊥. Lean’s map denotes the image subgroup. Preservation proves one inclusion; surjectivity supplies preimages for the reverse. Here Isometry includes a bijective group homomorphism, so the equality concerns the full target complement. This is transport of orthogonality for [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6)’s finite forms. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L765) passes.
The inverse-image formulation confirms both directions of transport.

A bijective pairing-preserving map carries nondegeneracy from A to B: pull two target elements back to A and compare their pairings against all source elements. Source nondegeneracy identifies the preimages. Here Isometry includes a group isomorphism, which is stronger than a merely preserving map; this is isomorphism invariance for [Nikulin §1.2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&option_lang=eng&paperid=1677&what=fullteng#page=6)’s finite forms. Existing [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Basic.lean#L402) passes.
Using the inverse gives the reverse implication as well.

A quadratic isometry is an additive bijection preserving q, hence its polar pairing b. It therefore transports both q-vanishing on H and the equality H=H⊥, exactly the two quadratic Lagrangian conditions. This matches [Nikulin §1.2–1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677), with q valued here in ℚ/ℤ after the half-norm conversion. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Metabolic.lean#L46) passes.
Forward and inverse transport of an existing quadratic Lagrangian preserve its existence.

A quadratic Lagrangian includes the condition q(x)=0 for every x in H, in addition to H=H⊥ for the polar pairing. This theorem extracts that supplied q-vanishing condition; it never infers it merely from vanishing of b. The distinction agrees with quadratic isotropy in [Nikulin §1.2–1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677). Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L593) passes.
The extracted subgroup condition gives q(x)=0 for every member; this control checks its elementwise meaning, not a direct use of the projection theorem.

The conclusion concerns the underlying polar pairing b: H equals its b-orthogonal complement. That equality is already a component of the supplied quadratic Lagrangian condition, alongside q-vanishing. Forgetting the quadratic condition is therefore valid even for degenerate forms. [Nikulin §1.2–1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677) distinguishes the quadratic form from its associated bilinear form. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Metabolic.lean#L37) passes.
An actual consumer uses this projection and explicit nondegeneracy to deduce square cardinality.

Here isotropy means q vanishes on the subgroup, with q in ℚ/ℤ. The additive equivalence preserves q, so its image has exactly the same quadratic values as the original subgroup. This specializes the preserving-map theorem to a bijection and matches the isometry convention of [Nikulin §1.2–1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677). Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L662) passes.
Quadratic isotropy transport combines with transport of polar self-orthogonality.

A Hom is an additive map preserving q, not necessarily an injection. Every element of the image subgroup has a preimage in H with the same q-value, so q vanishes on the image exactly when it vanishes on H. This directly matches quadratic isotropy in [Nikulin §1.2–1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677), including degenerate modules. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L584) passes.
The native isometry specialization checks the coercions and image subgroup convention.

If q vanishes on H, then b(x,y)=q(x+y)−q(x)−q(y)=0 for x,y∈H, since H is closed under addition. Thus every element of H belongs to H⊥ for b. This uses the full polar pairing from [Nikulin §1.2–1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677) after half-norm normalization; neither nondegeneracy nor division by two is required. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L635) passes.
The native polar-vanishing theorem proves the equivalent bilinear-isotropy formulation; this is a companion control rather than a direct consumer.

The hypothesis says q vanishes on H; the conclusion says its polar pairing b vanishes on H×H. Subgroup closure makes q(x+y), q(x), and q(y) all zero, so their difference is zero. This is the polarization formula of [Nikulin §1.2–1.4](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1677) in the half-norm convention, valid without nondegeneracy or division by two. Native [check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FiniteBilinearModule/Quadratic.lean#L684) passes.
An actual consumer combines the resulting bilinear isotropy with nondegeneracy and the precise cardinality condition.

This extends an additive monoid by a negation operation and subtraction defined by a−b=a+(−b). Integer multiples use repeated addition and negate positive multiples for negative integers. Negation is not required to be a genuine additive inverse, so familiar group identities such as a−a=0 are not asserted. Compared with [the reference](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Group/DivInvMonoid.lean#L175).

This additive monoid has involutive negation, the reversed-sum law −(a+b)=−b+−a, and the implication a+b=0 ⇒ −a=b. These agree with group laws, but do not require every element to cancel its negation. The source explicitly presents this as a weaker intermediate structure, not an additive group. Compared with [the reference](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Group/DivInvMonoid.lean#L305).

This adds commutative addition to a monoid with subtraction: negation is involutive, reverses sums, and identifies an inverse whenever a sum is zero. It agrees with these laws in abelian groups but still does not require a+(−a)=0. Thus the name does not silently impose an additive group. Compared with [the reference](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Group/DivInvMonoid.lean#L345).

An additive subgroup is a subset containing zero and closed under addition and additive inverses, exactly the usual subgroup criterion. Its operations are inherited from the ambient additive group. Commutativity is not required, and the trivial subgroup and whole group are allowed; the empty subset is excluded by zero membership. Compared with [the reference](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Group/Subgroup/Defs.lean#L302).

This property says that each subset in a specified family contains zero and is closed under addition and negation. In an additive group these are precisely the subgroup conditions. Lean also permits an ambient monoid with a weaker negation operation; there the assertion only records these closure conditions, without manufacturing inverses. Compared with [the reference](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Group/Subgroup/Defs.lean#L114).

This property requires every subset in a specified family to contain zero and be closed under addition. For additive monoids it is exactly the usual submonoid condition. Associativity is unnecessary for expressing these closure laws, so Lean only assumes addition has an identity. The family itself may be empty. Compared with [the reference](https://www.irif.fr/~jep/PDF/MPRI/MPRI.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Group/Submonoid/Defs.lean#L117).

This is the finite sum of f(i), with each index in the finite set counted once. Equal values at different indices are still counted separately. Associativity and commutativity make the order irrelevant, and the empty sum is zero. No convergence or infinite-summation convention enters this definition. Compared with [the reference](https://linear.axler.net/LADR4e.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/BigOperators/Group/Finset/Defs.lean#L67).

Multiplication by a strictly positive element on the left preserves strict inequalities: b<c implies a*b<a*c when 0<a. This isolates the familiar positive-multiplication rule. A preorder and a multiplication operation suffice to state it; commutativity, associativity and a corresponding right-multiplication rule are not assumed. Compared with [the reference](https://public.csusm.edu/aitken_html/m378_summer2019/Ch8SequencesLimits.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/GroupWithZero/Defs.lean#L107).

Multiplication by a strictly positive element on the right preserves strict inequalities: a<b implies a*c<b*c when 0<c. This is the right-hand version of the usual positive-multiplication rule. It remains distinct from the left-hand property when multiplication is noncommutative, and it requires no total order or associativity. Compared with [the reference](https://public.csusm.edu/aitken_html/m378_summer2019/Ch8SequencesLimits.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/GroupWithZero/Defs.lean#L139).

Every element of a group multiplied by its inverse gives the identity: a*a⁻¹=1. The source derives this right-inverse law from its chosen left-inverse axiom and associativity. No commutativity is needed. There is no nonzero premise because the group structure already makes every element invertible. Compared with [the reference](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Group/Defs.lean#L62).

Dividing by one leaves an element unchanged. Here division means multiplication by the supplied inverse, and the inverse of one is explicitly required to be one. Those assumptions suffice even when other elements lack genuine inverses; no field, commutativity or cancellation hypothesis is hidden. Compared with [the reference](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Group/Basic.lean#L353).

Subtracting an element from itself in an additive group gives zero. Subtraction here is defined as adding the additive inverse, so a−a=a+(−a)=0. The ambient addition need not be commutative. This uses genuine group inverses, rather than merely an arbitrarily supplied negation operation. Compared with [the reference](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Group/Defs.lean#L66).

Subtracting zero leaves an element unchanged. The hypotheses say that subtraction is addition of a supplied negation and that negating zero gives zero. These are enough for a−0=a+0=a; arbitrary elements need not possess genuine additive inverses, and commutativity is unnecessary. Compared with [the reference](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Group/Basic.lean#L353).

Subtracting a from zero gives its supplied negation: 0−a=−a. This follows from defining subtraction as addition of negation and from zero being an additive identity. The result does not require negation to be a genuine inverse, to be involutive, or even to fix zero. Compared with [the reference](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Group/DivInvMonoid.lean#L255).

Multiplying a vector by the sum of two scalars equals the sum of the two scalar multiples: (r+s)•x=r•x+s•x. This is the scalar-addition distributive law for a semimodule. Lean calls these structures modules even over semirings, so additive inverses of scalars or vectors are not required. Compared with [the reference](https://ftp.gwdg.de/pub/EMIS/journals/TAC/volumes/28/4/28-04.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Module/Defs.lean#L73).

For the scalar multiplication defined by ordinary multiplication itself, a•b equals a*b. The declaration makes that convention explicit; it does not assert that an arbitrary action on the same set must equal multiplication. No associativity or identity is needed for this basic operation-level equality. Compared with [the reference](https://www.irif.fr/~jep/PDF/MPRI/MPRI.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Group/Action/Defs.lean#L72).

The sum of two nonnegative elements is nonnegative. It is enough that adding a fixed element on the left preserves the preorder: from 0≤b obtain a≤a+b, then combine with 0≤a. Neither commutativity nor associativity, subtraction or a total order is required. Compared with [the reference](https://public.csusm.edu/aitken_html/m378_summer2019/Ch8SequencesLimits.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Monoid/Unbundled/Basic.lean#L747).

The distinguished element one differs from zero under the explicit hypothesis that one is nonzero. This is an exposed assumption, not a theorem excluding the zero ring without a hypothesis. No ring operations or characteristic-zero assumption are required; only the two designated elements and their inequality are used. Compared with [the reference](https://public.csusm.edu/aitken_html/m378_summer2019/Ch8SequencesLimits.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/NeZero.lean#L34).

The function that takes value x at index i and zero elsewhere takes value zero at every different index i′. The inequality hypothesis is essential. The coordinate sets may vary with the index; only a designated zero in each coordinate and decidable equality of indices are needed. Compared with [the reference](https://linear.axler.net/LADR4e.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Notation/Pi/Basic.lean#L36).

The function with value x at index i and zero elsewhere evaluates to x at i. This is the defining coordinate rule behind a vector supported at one index. It remains valid for arbitrary index sets and varying coordinate types; neither a finite index set nor a vector-space structure is required. Compared with [the reference](https://linear.axler.net/LADR4e.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Notation/Pi/Basic.lean#L33).

Second countability means that the topology has a countable basis, as in Semmes. The definition stores a countable family generating the topology; taking finite intersections converts it into a countable basis. Thus the formulation has the usual meaning, and countable includes finite families and the empty space. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L788).

First countability requires a countable neighborhood basis at every point, exactly Semmes’s local condition. The neighborhood-filter formulation says every neighborhood contains one from a countable generating family; interiors give an open neighborhood basis. The family can depend on the point, and the empty space satisfies the condition vacuously. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L714).

A separable space has a countable dense subset, matching Semmes’s definition exactly. Dense means that every nonempty open set meets that subset. Countable includes finite and empty sets, so the empty space is separable. Neither a metric nor a sequence converging to every point is required. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L346).

This documented predicate requires s to lie in the closure of a countable ambient set. That witnessing set need not lie inside s, so this is weaker than separability of the subspace in general. The distinction from Semmes’s ordinary separability is explicit; for the whole space the definitions agree. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L504).

Every space with a countable topological basis has a countable dense subset. Choose one point from each nonempty basis element; every nonempty open set contains such an element and therefore meets the chosen set. This is precisely Semmes’s proof, with no metric, Hausdorffness, or nonemptiness assumption on the space. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L911).

This chooses a countable topological basis from the existence guaranteed by second countability. The chosen basis omits the empty set, which does not affect the unions generating open sets. It is an arbitrary classical choice rather than a canonical enumeration; in the empty space the basis itself is empty. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L821).

The chosen countable family is a genuine basis: its members cover the space, and near a point the intersection of two members contains another member. Its generated topology is the original topology. These conditions recover Semmes’s characterization that every open set is a union of basis members. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L833).

A separable space supplies a countable subset whose closure is the whole space. This exposes exactly the witness in Semmes’s definition, without selecting an enumeration or claiming that the ambient set is countable. Empty spaces are included, while a dense sequence requires the separate nonemptiness assumption used by the companion theorem. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L350).

Every nonempty separable space admits a sequence with dense range. Enumerate a countable dense set, allowing repetitions when it is finite. The explicit nonemptiness assumption matters: there is no function from the natural numbers into the empty space. Density of the range does not assert convergence of the sequence. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L365).

The product of two spaces with countable bases again has a countable basis. Take all products of one basis member from each factor; these rectangles form a basis for the product topology and are indexed by a countable product. This matches Semmes’s finite-product construction and allows empty factors. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L901).

A product indexed by a countable set of spaces with countable bases has a countable basis. Basic open sets restrict only finitely many coordinates, giving a countable collection of finite choices. This matches Semmes’s countable-product construction. Finite index sets are allowed; an empty index set gives a singleton product. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L906).

The product of two first-countable spaces is first countable. At a pair of points, products of members of their countable neighborhood bases form a countable neighborhood basis for the product topology. This is Semmes’s local product construction. No countable basis for either whole space is assumed. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L770).

A countable product of first-countable spaces is first countable. At any product point, combine countable local bases using restrictions in finitely many coordinates. There are countably many such choices, and they refine every product neighborhood, as in Semmes’s construction. This includes finite products and the singleton product with no factors. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L776).

The product of two separable spaces is separable. The product of their countable dense subsets is countable and dense, since every nonempty basic open rectangle meets it. This follows from Semmes’s separability definition and closure-of-products formula. Neither second countability nor nonempty factors are required. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L429).

A countable product of separable spaces is separable. In a nonempty product, fix a base point and vary finitely many coordinates through countable dense subsets. These finite modifications form a countable dense set because product neighborhoods restrict finitely many coordinates. The zero-factor product and empty factors are also included. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L435).

Every subspace of a space with a countable basis has a countable basis in its inherited topology. Intersect the ambient basis elements with the subset; these intersections generate exactly the relative open sets. This is Semmes’s subspace-basis result, with no openness, closedness, or nonemptiness requirement on the subset. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L890).

If a domain’s topology is exactly pulled back from a second-countable target along a map, the domain is second countable. Preimages of a countable target basis give a countable domain basis. This extends Semmes’s subspace construction to arbitrary maps; injectivity is unnecessary, because fibers may contain topologically indistinguishable points. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L1173).

If a dense subset s is itself separable with its inherited topology, it contains a countable subset dense in the whole space. Choose a countable set dense in s and use transitivity of density. The separability assumption is on s itself, not merely on the surrounding space. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L671).

In a space with a countable basis, any union of open sets equals a union of countably many sets from the same family. Choose one covering set for each relevant basis element, exactly as in Semmes’s Lindelöf theorem. The family need not cover the whole space, and an empty family is allowed. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L929).

In a separable space, a pairwise disjoint family of sets with nonempty interiors has only countably many indices. Choose a point of a countable dense set inside each interior; disjointness makes these choices distinct. The sets need not be open, but nonempty interior is essential to the argument. [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf); [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Topology/Bases.lean#L494).
